4.text: While the dance is being performed, the other dancers remain quiet, and

5.text: look on together with the spectators. After the dance, the man must give

6.text: some present to the woman; and the following night they sleep together,

7.text: leaving their respective mates to arrange matters between themselves. On

8.text: the next day, the husband of the woman, and the wife of the man, perform a

9.text: similar dance, in which the man gives an equivalent of the present of the

10.text: day before; and each newly-mated couple sleeps together for another night.

11.text: Such dances are arranged chiefly among cousins or other relatives, who, among

12.text: the Chukchee, frequently assume the bond of compound marriage. Conversely,

13.text: a new bond of compound marriage may be concluded through a trading-

14.text: dance. This is closely analogous to the customs of the Alaskan Eskimo as

15.text: described by Nelson;¹ but with the Chukchee an exchange of wives leads, as

16.text: a rule, to the lasting bond of compound marriage, or to what is so called.

17.text: So often is this the case, that even the women who mix with the sailors from

18.text: whaling-ships consider them their husbands by compound marriage. Among

19.text: the Chukchee, clandestine intercourse with another man’s wife is called by the

20.text: same name. When the affair first comes to the knowledge of the husband,

23.text: CEREMONIALS OF ASIATIC ESKIMO. Ceremonial of Kaˊcak. — Among

24.text: the Asiatic Eskimo the ceremonial of the winter is connected in most villages,

25.text: not with Kereˊtkun, but with the Big-Woman. Some families in the villages

26.text: Wuteˊen and Iˊwtun, however, connect the ceremonial with Kereˊtkun, who

27.text: is called by them Kaˊcak. The name of Kaˊcak as identical with Kereˊtkun

28.text: is known also in Uñiˊsak and on St. Lawrence Island. In Uñiˊsak, some

29.text: families are said to perform a simple “genuine thanksgiving” ceremonial

30.text: analogous. to that of the Maritime Chukchee. The ceremonial of Kaˊcak or of

31.text: Big-Woman is performed with the same details as that of Kereˊtkun among

32.text: the Chukchee. Even the net, the wooden birds, and the painted paddles² are

33.text: of exactly the same character. The differences have already been referred.
